title: Curve add-liquidity is charged against the swap rate limit as well as the deposit limit, because an imbalanced deposit is economically a swap
content:
A.6.1.1.2.2.6.1.2.2.1.2.1.2.8.2.5 decreases `LIMIT_CURVE_DEPOSIT` by the aggregated `valueDeposited` before liquidity is added. Then A...8.2.7 does something less obvious: it also decreases `LIMIT_CURVE_SWAP`, by an amount it calls `averageSwap`, computed *after* the deposit from the difference between what was deposited and the pro-rata pool composition the minted shares entitle the proxy to:

```
totalSwapped += MathLib._absSubtraction(
    curvePool.balances(i) * rates[i] * shares / curvePool.totalSupply(),
    params.depositAmounts[i] * rates[i]
);
uint256 averageSwap = totalSwapped / 2 / 1e18;
```

The insight is that a single-sided or skewed deposit into a StableSwap pool is a swap wearing a deposit's clothes: you hand over one asset and end up with a claim on a basket. Without this second charge, a relayer with an exhausted `LIMIT_CURVE_SWAP` could keep converting assets indefinitely by depositing imbalanced and later withdrawing balanced.

The division by two is the tell that the quantity is deliberately an *average* of the two legs — the same notional is counted once as sold and once as bought, so charging the full `totalSwapped` would double-bill.

This is the strongest general lesson in the chunk: rate limits must be keyed to **economic effect**, not to function name. Any limit taxonomy organised by entry point rather than by outcome is bypassable by choosing a differently-named door to the same result.
description: The imbalance between deposits and the pro-rata value of minted shares is computed as an implied averageSwap, closing a route that would let a relayer swap without touching the swap limit.
